The reason the FTC is blocking the merger has nothing to do with small and medium size business which have a huge number of options in buying office supplies. Everything from large retailers like Walmart to Amazon, to the smaller independent dealers, of which there are probably dozens if you are in a larger metro area. The reason they are blocking the merger is because of the Fortune 1000 companies and federal government contracts.

No other companies are suited to serve corporations of that size and be competitive on the national (and international) scale. You can point to Amazon and Walmart, but in truth the pricing they offer isn't even close to competitive with Staples, Depot, or the independent dealers when it comes to the high volume items those large entities need to run. How is Amazon going to have a truckload of paper delivered? How is Walmart going to have 25 offices of furniture delivered and installed?

Independent dealers are competitive with Staples and Depot, but lack the nationwide logistics to handle the contracts of the size that some of these companies dictate. The largest independent dealer is W.B. Mason. They have a large presence in the northeast, but little to none in the south, mid-west, and western US. So a nationwide contract can be nearly impossible to be profitable on if you don't have the logistics assets in place on a nationwide scale. Paying a courier service or freight company is several times more expensive in most cases than having your own delivery fleet taking care of deliveries for you.

The industry wholesalers (Essendant and SPRichards) who do have the logistics chains in place to handle these sorts of contracts have no interest in getting involved with fulfillment to the end user, and prefer to stay wholesalers. Word was that Essendant was in talks with Staples to take over some of the large contracts and have a network of independent dealers fulfill them. So far nothing has come of this.
